comment_grading:
Lab gradings are based on strict marking scheme. No room for argument mostly. Not difficult to get full mark for all the labs if you follow through the instructions and tested the code before submission. No late submission allowed.
Midterms and finals are both pretty difficult this year (judged from mean score and SD). The reading-load during exam is extremely huge and the time is VERY tight. No breathing moment definitely. Both of them are divided into two sections (no significant difference in difficulty). Also, both open book, feel free to read any downloaded PDF sources or Python files from your computer, as well as the course website).
Midterm: 25 mins per section, approx. 9 questions per section.
Final: 40 mins per section, approx. 10 questions per section.
Each question may have the length of up to a page or two (for final even THREE!) and you NEED time to digest what the code is trying to do. Most questions are about filling a gap in the code so it works as intended or something like that. Not difficult if given enough time but you just don't have that luxury. All in all I find it a reading comprehension and common sense exam undercovered as Python.
Midterm CAN be omitted as there are two formulae for grading but not recommend to skip midterm since final could be even harder. Just don't bet.
Use of formula:
(Lab + Midterm + Final)
Formula 1:
36%+24%+40%
Formula 2:
42%+0%+58%
Automatically applies the higher one.
Grades (which you care about):
Lab:
Me = 100/100 (100,100,100)
Average mean = 93.67
Midterm:
Me = 82/100 (+1.09 SD)
Mean = 54.6
SD = 25.1
Final:
Me = 84/100 (+1.45 SD)
Mean = 55.5
SD = 19.6
Overall = 90.72/100 (Formula 2)
Grade = A+
A-range is highly competitive and there will always be people ahead of you unless you scored full mark for everything. I guess this year A-range was loosen (since Rossiter is leaving) but you better score more SD than me for good grades. I think from what I heard A+ cutoff is 90 this year (lucky me).

comment_content:
Format:
Lectures: 2 sessions per week, around 1 hour each; attendance not counted.
Lectures only use PowerPoint slides from the course website, which are updated weekly.
A textbook written by the lecturer (《Interactive Python Programming for Beginners》, September 2016, around $190) is recommended but not required to complete the assessments.
Labs: 1 session per week, around 2 hours each, attendance not counted.
Labs only use materials from the course website, with a lab task for each session.
Except for the labs required for assignments, no other labs need to be submitted or graded.
Course Coverage: (textbook chapter numbers in brackets)
Programming fundamentals and basic Python functions (03,05,07)
Basic conditional statements (if...elif...else), loops (while, for...in) (05,06)
Basic drawing functions in the Turtle library (02)
Drawing with Turtle using loops (06)
PyGame library's MIDI functionality and time control (time.sleep())
Data Structures: List, Tuple, Dictionary (08)
List and String: Slicing and basic functions (append(), insert(), remove(), extend(), reverse(), ...) (08)
Function structure and operations, global vs local variables, stack, recursion (09)
type(), file read/write (04,13)
Dictionary structure and operations (10)
Dynamic Turtle operations and settings: speed(), tracer(), reset(), shape(), shapesize(), ontimer(), update(), ... (11,12)
Turtle mouse and keyboard event control (12)
Class and Objects (14)
As an introductory course, it is reasonable not to cover all Python features comprehensively (e.g. with..., lambda, exception)

The Python library turtle was an engaging and surprisingly effective tool for the course. At first glance, it seemed like a basic graphics tool for beginners, but it proved to be much more than that. By using turtle, we were able to visually understand programming concepts such as loops, functions, and even event-driven programming, which made the learning process both interactive and enjoyable.
One of the standout aspects of learning with turtle was its ability to train a programmer's mindset. It encouraged logical thinking, problem-solving, and debugging, as we had to figure out how to make the turtle move in specific patterns. The process of troubleshooting errors and refining code to create precise results felt similar to real-world programming challenges, which added depth to the learning experience.
Overall, the course successfully used turtle to not only teach Python basics but also to develop a strong foundation in programming logic and creativity. I would recommend this course to anyone starting their journey in programming or looking for a fun way to strengthen their skills.

comment_content:
The course is called introduction to programming, but in fact the people taking the course typically already know Java or another programming language. If you are truly looking for an introductory programming class, I recommend COMP1021 instead.
The exam papers are far too easy, but there are many tricks that make you lose points. I find these tricks rather pointless, as any free IDE should be able to catch such errors with ease. They include:
- Hidden curly brackets or syntax errors in the LQs
- Poorly phrased questions (eg. how many times is a function called?)
- Easily testable things not taught in lectures (eg. float multiplied by an integer)
None of the content is particularly hard. The course will cover basic variables, conditional statements, expressions, looping, recursion, classes and inheritance, 1D and 2D arrays, and basic data structures (stack and queue). 
If you want to do well, just make sure you do not make any careless mistakes. I have heard that even a 90% is B range in this class.
Overall, I learned very little from this class, and the exam was more focused on trying to trick you rather than testing your ability to think like a programmer.

However, as I have a background in programming (as do the majority of people taking this course), he goes far too slowly for my liking (for reference, I only write a few lines of notes per lecture). He does go through examples in his classes, but they are far too basic to be of much use. 
If you have a background in programming, I recommend skipping his lectures and revising the material per the slides instead.
Both of the TAs for this course are very competent. During labs, they readily go around the lecture hall to answer any questions. Moreover, they mark labs, assignments, and exam papers at an astonishing pace. I cannot commend them enough.
comment_grading:
Two pathways for grading:
10% labs, 5% written assignment, 20% programming assignment
If midterm score > final score: 25% midterm, 40% final

comment_teaching:
Raymond is an exceptional teacher. After each lesson, he stays to clarify any confusion regarding the course material, ensuring that every question is answered before the session ends. If any questions arise after class, students can easily reach him via email, and he responds with detailed and thorough explanations promptly.
A unique aspect of the course is the "coupon" policy, which has two main uses:
Assignment Waiver: The coupon can be used to waive one question on an assignment, granting full points regardless of whether the answer is correct or even submitted. This is particularly useful if you're struggling with a specific question or if you're racing against the deadline and can't complete all the tasks (not that anyone would have personal experience with that).
Project Advantage: It can also secure full marks on one part of a project, which might otherwise be challenging to achieve without utilizing the coupon.
Coupons can primarily be earned in two ways: by answering questions posed by Raymond during lessons or by providing solutions for the "in-class exercise" (which will be further discussed in the 'workload' section). However, if you’re hesitant about answering questions quickly or feel unsure about completing the "in-class" exercises, there’s no need to worry. As the semester progresses, Raymond will inquire whether students have coupons. For those who do not, he will offer opportunities to answer questions, making it highly likely that everyone will earn at least one coupon, which is especially encouraged for use in projects.

comment_workload:
The workload for this course is manageable, comprising only two homework assignments and one project over the semester.
Homework
There are two homework assignments: one before the midterm exam and one afterward. Each assignment consists of four to five questions that assess your understanding of the course material. For someone like me, who tends to learn the material while doing homework, it takes about five hours to complete each assignment—roughly one hour per question. This is relatively light compared to the two-month deadlines for each assignment.
Project
The bulk of the course workload is centered around the project, which can be completed individually or in pairs. The project consists of three phases, and as long as you follow Raymond's guidance, achieving a full score is quite feasible. In fact, the average score for the project is over 90%. As a solo participant, I spent about three days on the project, which may sound like a lot, but is actually quite light given the generous deadlines.
In-Class Exercises (Optional)
Raymond offers in-class exercises during lessons, which are discussed in the following class. If you feel confident, you can arrive a bit early to show your answers to Raymond. If your answer is correct, you can earn a "coupon." However, participation in these exercises is entirely optional; I personally never participated in them before exam revisions.
Attendance
During lessons, there are iPRS questions that grant you marks simply for participating, regardless of whether your answers are correct.
